title: About this site
text:
How the tools work
Each tool is a small program. When you open a tool, the program is downloaded into your browser and runs on your own device. That is why the first visit takes a little longer.

The numbers you enter and the sliders you move stay on your device. They are not sent to a server.
You need no account and no login.
The site sets no cookies.

title: About this site
text:
What is recorded
Hosting. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. As with any website, the host’s servers receive your IP address when your browser requests a page. GitHub describes what it does with this in its privacy statement.
Visit counter. The site counts how often each page is opened, using GoatCounter. For each visit the counter records the page, the country, the type of browser and device, the screen size, the browser language, and the page you came from. It sets no cookies, does not store your IP address, and builds no profile of you. The counts tell me which tools are used; they do not tell me who used them or what was entered.
Feedback form. The “Feedback” link opens a form on Google Forms. Using it is voluntary. The form asks for no name and no email address; what you write is visible only to me. Google’s privacy policy applies to the form.

title: Antitrust Lab
text: Change the inputs, watch the outcome, and test the economics behind competition law. Each tool runs in your browser: no installation, no login. The first visit takes a little longer while the tool loads.

title: For instructors
text: Each tool follows the same layout: a question, a few controls with presets, one main chart, number tiles, and a verdict phrased as the legal test. An Experiments tab asks students to predict before they reveal the answer; a Model tab gives the formulas and sources.

title: For instructors
text:
Using a tool in class

Open the tool before the session; the first load downloads the R runtime into the browser.
Start from the default preset, which matches the standard textbook example.
Ask the room to predict the effect of one change, then move the slider.

title: For instructors
text:
Monopoly and welfare








Tab
Concept
Teaching point




1 Monopoly and deadweight loss
Monopoly Pricing and Welfare; Deadweight Loss (DWL)
The monopolist cuts output; part of the lost consumer surplus is a transfer, the rest is lost to everyone


2 Rent seeking
Rent Seeking; Rent Seeking and the Social Cost of Monopoly
If firms spend resources to win the monopoly, the social cost is the triangle plus part of the rents

title: For instructors
text:
How many firms?








Tab
Concept
Teaching point




1 The trade-off
Model: Cournot Competition with n Firms; Model: Consumer Surplus and Profits
More firms lower the price but each one duplicates the fixed cost; consumers and society can prefer different numbers


2 Fixed costs and market structure
Fixed Costs and the Optimal Number of Firms; Model: The Optimal Number of Firms
High fixed costs support few firms; free entry can bring more firms than welfare calls for


3 Price competition
Extension beyond the slides: differentiated products, firms set prices
How firms compete after entry decides how many enter: soft competition attracts too many firms, tough competition can leave too few

title: For instructors
text:
Market definition








Tab
Concept
Teaching point




1 Is a price increase profitable?
Critical Loss; Predicting the Loss: Two Routes; Whole Foods/Wild Oats
High margins lower the critical loss; margins and elasticities must fit together


2 SSNIP step by step
SSNIP Test: Steps; Running Case: Nestlé/Perrier
Widen the candidate market until the price increase is profitable


3 Cellophane fallacy
The Cellophane Fallacy
At the monopoly price the test always fails, so start from a competitive price

title: For instructors
text:
Concentration and market power








Tab
Concept
Teaching point




1 Shares and markups
Lerner Index; Formal Steps for Indirect Approach; Industry-Wide Lerner Index
In Cournot, L = s/|η|; the same shares mean less market power when demand is more elastic


2 HHI and the merger screen
HHI; CR4; What Do Thresholds Actually Mean in Law?
Compute HHI and its change; US presumption vs. EU safe harbour (Heinz/Beech-Nut)


3 Is concentration market power?
High HHI Is Neither Necessary Nor Sufficient
The same HHI gives zero (Bertrand), Cournot or monopoly markups


4 Beyond HHI: diversion and GUPPI
Beyond HHI: Diversion Ratios; From Diversion Ratios to Pricing Pressure
HHI and GUPPI can disagree in both directions; diversion where the competition takes place
